solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One resisting reforms in biblical texts: curbs upset opponents

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged
the following word group is placed inside the scripture abbreviation, as if written in it

parts.note: OT, the Old Testament, the biblical texts before the Gospels
the word curbs, rearranged
antis are people who are against something

explanation.surface: A conservative cleric fights changes to scripture by ranting that upset rivals are curbing it.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-letter scripture abbreviation opens around the rest: the jumbled curbs followed by the opponents.
explanation.definitionFit: An obscurantist deliberately opposes enlightenment and progress, so is someone resisting reform.

clue.text: Redeployment of Paul to fix, arrangement following redundancy?

indicators.note: redeploying moves staff into new positions, so the letters take new places

parts.note: the two words, rearranged
to cement is to fix firmly

explanation.surface: Paul is being moved to another post to sort things out after job cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redeployment' looks like the definition, which suits the surface, but it is the anagram signal; the definition is the closing phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Outplacement is the service of helping redundant employees find new jobs, an arrangement made after laying them off.

clue.text: Old lists — artist turned up in a couple

indicators.note: the painter goes inside the word for a pair

parts.note: a brace is a pair, as of game birds

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means read from the bottom upward, so backwards

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, the standard crossword artist

explanation.surface: Antique registers show a painter appearing among a pair of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lists' is not a set of records but the barriers enclosing a jousting ground, an old sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrace is an obsolete word for the barrier of a tournament ground, the lists where knights jousted.

clue.text: Part of old NCO's rank, a short time abandoning lines, ideas changing

indicators.note: ideas that are changing take a different form, so the letters reorder
abandoning means leaving behind, so the two line abbreviations are dropped

parts.note: a spell is a short period
L stands for line, twice for lines
the word ideas, rearranged

explanation.surface: A former soldier's rank briefly drops its lines as thinking about it shifts.
explanation.walkthrough: SPELL loses both Ls, then the shuffled ideas follow to make SPEISADE.
explanation.definitionFit: Speisade, as in lance-speisade, is an obsolete term for the lowest grade of non-commissioned officer, a lance corporal.

clue.text: What'll frame unusual image? This could shed light, bizarrely

indicators.note: the frame of a word is its border, so only its first and last letters are wanted

parts.note: the two letters at the edges of the word
an icon is an image

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what will frame a strange picture, and a light source.
explanation.walkthrough: The ulicon is a fish; 'bizarrely' flags that it sheds light in an odd way, being so oily it can be dried and burnt as a candle.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulicon or candlefish of the North Pacific is so rich in oil that it has served as a natural candle.

clue.text: One of the viols — who'd mutiny with base doubled?

indicators.note: in a down entry the base is the bottom letter, and doubling that Roman numeral swaps in its double

parts.note: a rebel is one who would mutiny

explanation.surface: Asks which stringed instrument would rebel, playing on a doubled bass line.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of REBEL is L, the Roman 50; doubled it is 100, C. 'Base' sounds like the bass of a viol, a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: The rebec is a medieval bowed stringed instrument, counted among the early members of the viol family.

clue.text: Name copying old table linen

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for name
apery is an old word for mimicry, aping

explanation.surface: Someone names a person copying old-fashioned tablecloths.
explanation.definitionFit: Napery is household linen, especially tablecloths and napkins.

clue.text: Gum, often sweet round its centre

indicators.note: going round something encloses it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a tart is often a sweet pastry

indicators.note: the centre of the first word is its single middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of the three

explanation.surface: Chewing gum, often sweet, has a soft middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gum' is both the definition and, through 'its', the word whose centre is put inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuart is a Western Australian eucalyptus, and eucalyptuses are called gum trees.

clue.text: Witness the arrival of bishop's former throne at home (5, two words)

parts.note: a see was originally a bishop's seat or throne
in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone watches a bishop's old throne being delivered to the house.
explanation.definitionFit: To see in the New Year is to stay up and witness its arrival.

clue.text: Unusual veg changes colour — one's peering nervously inside (12, two words)

parts.note: surface padding: it dresses up the vegetable and gives no letters

indicators.note: the jumbled word sits within the word for changing colour

parts.note: leaves turn when they change colour

indicators.note: acting nervously means jittery and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the word peering, rearranged

explanation.surface: A strange vegetable changes colour as someone peers at it nervously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' is surface colour only, and 'colour' wants to be GREEN on its own; it belongs with 'changes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Turnip greens are the leafy tops of turnips, eaten as a cooked vegetable.

clue.text: Lip applied to drink pages brought in as accompaniment for roast (10, two words)

indicators.note: something brought in is placed inside, here inside the drink

parts.note: ale is a drink
pp is the abbreviation for pages
lip and sauce both mean cheek, impudence

explanation.surface: Someone puts their lips to a drink while pages are fetched to go with the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'applied to' places the cheek after the drink with its pages inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple sauce is the traditional condiment served with roast pork.

clue.text: Terrier really expecting you? Heads for leash

indicators.note: heads are the front ends, so the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the initials of the four words

explanation.surface: A dog owner asks the eager terrier whether it is waiting for its walk lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leash' looks like a dog's lead, but in hunting a leash is a set of three hounds or hares.
explanation.definitionFit: A trey is a three in cards or dice, and a leash is likewise a group of three.

clue.text: Geological feature that arises from retreating glacier and leaves sand in rising incline

definitions.text: Geological feature that arises from retreating glacier

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom upward, so backwards
to leave something in a place is to deposit it there, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a rake is a slope or incline, as of a stage
S is the abbreviation for sand

explanation.surface: A glacier retreats and leaves sand on a rising slope, as glaciers do.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is long, and its 'retreating' tempts a reversal there; the reversal is signalled by 'rising' instead.
explanation.definitionFit: An eskar (esker) is a long winding ridge of gravel deposited by meltwater beneath a retreating glacier.

clue.text: Document? Copy deposited with letters for…

indicators.note: something deposited with something else is lodged inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: the abbreviation for the next clue's answer, which the ellipsis points to
to ape is to copy

explanation.surface: A copied document is lodged along with letters addressed to someone, the sentence trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into 14 across: 'letters for' that answer means its standard two-letter abbreviation, Pr for Prince.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper is a written document, as in official papers.

clue.text: …This member of royal family, new in charge

indicators.note: one piece sits within the word for a charge

parts.note: a price is a charge
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Continuing from 13 across: letters for a new royal who has taken charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' refers back to the previous clue, whose letters were addressed to this royal.
explanation.definitionFit: A prince is a son or close male relative of a monarch, so a member of a royal family.

clue.text: Fine rain? Get dry at home

parts.note: sere means dry and withered
in means at home

explanation.surface: Drizzling outside? Then stay home and keep dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Serein is the fine rain that falls from a clear sky after sunset.

clue.text: Little girl, foolish one cutting ringlet

indicators.note: a thing cutting into another goes inside it, splitting it in two

parts.note: a lock is a curl of hair, like a ringlet
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A small girl, a silly thing, chops off one of her curls.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Scots: -ock is a diminutive ending, so a lassock is a little lass.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassock is a Scots word for a young girl, a diminutive of lass.

clue.text: Temple gateway, enormous, abandoned by king, faulty inside

indicators.note: the faulty word is placed within what remains
what is abandoned by someone is left without them, so that word is dropped

parts.note: plonking is informal for very large
taken as written
ropy means poor in quality, faulty

explanation.surface: A huge temple gate, deserted by its king, is defective within.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole word KING is removed from PLONKING, not just its abbreviation K.
explanation.definitionFit: A propylon is the monumental gateway in front of an ancient Egyptian temple.

clue.text: Take back one woollen fabric no longer in use

parts.note: 'un is a dialect form of one, as in 'a good 'un'

parts.words: woollen fabric no longer in use
parts.note: say is an obsolete fine serge cloth

explanation.surface: Return one woollen garment that has gone out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no longer in use' marks the cloth as archaic, though it reads as an unwanted garment.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsay something is to retract or withdraw a statement already made.

clue.text: Israeli, one born in a stretch of his homeland

indicators.note: the two short pieces go within the kept section
a stretch is only a section, so letters at both ends are dropped and a run from the middle is kept

parts.note: the Israeli's homeland
a means one
b is the abbreviation for born

explanation.surface: An Israeli native, born in a particular stretch of his own country.
explanation.walkthrough: Only SRA is taken from the inside of ISRAEL, with A and B placed in it; the wordplay also describes what a sabra is.
explanation.definitionFit: A sabra is a Jew born in Israel, as opposed to an immigrant, named after a local prickly-pear cactus.

clue.text: Weakling died, suitable inscription appended

indicators.note: something appended is added at the end, so this piece follows the first

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for died
RIP, rest in peace, the usual gravestone inscription

explanation.surface: A feeble person died, and a fitting epitaph was added.
explanation.definitionFit: A drip is informal for a dull, feeble, ineffectual person.

clue.text: I'll join regiment under canvas, on the move

definitions.note: this fits ITINERANT; ITERANT means repeating

indicators.note: will join says the first-person piece is attached to what comes next

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: being under canvas means being inside a tent, so the regiment goes within it

parts.note: a tent is made of canvas
RA, the Royal Artillery regiment

explanation.surface: A recruit says he will join a regiment living in tents and always moving on.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition seems a slip: 'on the move' suits ITINERANT, while Chambers gives ITERANT as repeating. The wordplay builds ITERANT cleanly.
explanation.definitionFit: Only loosely: iterant means repeating or recurring, and the travelling sense belongs to the similar word itinerant.

clue.text: Yield, or what yield comes from, we hear?

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling may differ from the word meant

parts.note: a crop's yield grows from seed

explanation.surface: A riddle playing on two senses of yield: giving way, and a harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yield' is used twice, once as the verb defined and once as the noun for a crop.
explanation.definitionFit: To cede is to give up or surrender, which is to yield.

clue.text: High churchman brought in to discharge church composer

indicators.note: the cleric's title is brought inside the word for discharge

parts.note: to discharge a debt is to pay it
RR, Right Reverend, the title of a bishop

explanation.surface: A senior cleric is called in to expel a church musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High churchman' suggests a ritualist, but means a cleric high in rank, styled Right Reverend.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Hubert Parry composed much church music, including the hymn tune for Jerusalem.

clue.text: Went through changes with beer in picnic basket?

indicators.note: the drink sits within the basket

parts.note: a ped is a basket or hamper
ale is beer

explanation.surface: Someone goes through mood swings, with beer packed in the picnic hamper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changes' is bell-ringing: a change is one ordering of the bells, and ringing through changes is what bells do.
explanation.definitionFit: Bells that pealed rang out in sequences called changes.

clue.text: Disowns Irish singer that's off-key

indicators.note: a singer off-key is out of tune, so the letters are put out of order

parts.note: surface padding that also flags the word's Irish usage; gives no letters
the word singer, rearranged

explanation.surface: A badly out-of-tune Irish vocalist is disowned.
explanation.walkthrough: Renig is a dialect form of renege, recorded in Irish use.
explanation.definitionFit: To renig is to renege, going back on a promise or disowning a commitment.

clue.text: Cry after whacking? Master going to head — bunk off

indicators.note: going to the head means being placed at the front, ahead of the other piece

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for master
what someone cries out when struck

explanation.surface: A pupil yelps after a caning, the master heads off, and the boy skips school.
explanation.walkthrough: To bunk off is British for playing truant.
explanation.definitionFit: Mouch, or mooch, means to skulk or play truant, as does bunking off.

clue.text: Sex counsellor? 'English must quit stays'

indicators.note: the letter that must quit leaves, so it is taken out

parts.note: Marie Stopes, the pioneer of birth control and sex advice
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A sex adviser declares that the English must abandon corsets.
explanation.walkthrough: Marie Stopes was a British campaigner for birth control and author of Married Love; 'stays' are corsets in the surface but the verb halts in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stays as a verb means halts or checks, and so does stops.

clue.text: Potential energy in rebel set off what may alert police

indicators.note: the physics abbreviation goes inside the rebel
something set off explodes, scattering it into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
PE is the physics abbreviation for potential energy

explanation.surface: A rebel's latent energy is triggered by a device that tips off the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' reads as the rebel's bomb or alarm going off, but it is the anagram signal for the combined letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A bleeper is a pager that emits a beep, a device that can summon someone such as a police officer.

clue.text: Access code: proceed northwards in queue (not east)

indicators.note: not east says the compass letter is removed
the backward word goes within the shortened queue

parts.note: a line is a queue

indicators.note: in a down entry, northwards means read from the bottom upward, so backwards

parts.note: to go is to proceed
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A computer access code tells you to move up the queue, without heading east.
explanation.definitionFit: A login is the username and password entry that gains access to a computer system.

clue.text: Bomb scrap left in ruin

indicators.note: the scrap goes inside the word for ruin

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or ruin
an ort is a scrap of food left over

explanation.surface: A bomb leaves scraps lying in the ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' belongs with 'scrap': an ort is a leftover, not L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortar bomb is the shell fired from a mortar, and mortar is used for the weapon and its bomb.

clue.text: Close to eponymous heroine, equivalent of one in Shakespeare?

parts.note: on can mean next to or close to
Jane Eyre is the heroine who gives the novel its title

explanation.surface: Something near a title heroine is like a figure in Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: Oneyre occurs once in Henry IV Part 1 and its meaning is guessed; it is taken as built on one, a person of a kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Oneyre is a Shakespearean nonce word usually explained as 'one' in the sense of a person or fellow.

clue.text: Antiseptic? Get that to apply for back!

indicators.note: going back means running the other way, so the joined pieces are read right to left

parts.note: lo! means look, as in 'get that!'
to sue for something is to petition or apply for it

explanation.surface: An instruction to fetch antiseptic and dab it on someone's back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get that' and 'apply' both suggest the treatment, but are the interjection and the legal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Eusol is a chlorinated lime solution once widely used to disinfect wounds, an antiseptic.

clue.text: What's maybe in Scots gin English too endlessly knocked back?

indicators.note: knocked back means turned the other way, so the pieces are read right to left
without its end, the word loses its last letter

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
also means too

explanation.surface: A Scottish drinker downs gin, and English gin too, as if knocking it back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests drinking the gin, but it reverses E plus ALS. Sloe gin is gin flavoured with sloes.
explanation.definitionFit: Slae is the Scots word for sloe, the blackthorn fruit steeped in gin to make sloe gin.

clue.text: Winter visitor to SA cruising in peace with P & O (good on board) (10, two words)

indicators.note: a passenger on board is inside the ship, so this letter goes within the shipping line
cruising means wandering about, so the letters move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the letters of the shipping company's name
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A winter tourist to South Africa sails peacefully with the P&O line, behaving well aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: P&O is a British shipping and cruise company. SA is South Africa, whose seas the bird visits.
explanation.definitionFit: The cape pigeon is a pied southern petrel that visits South African waters in winter.

clue.text: Afternoon events: these mostly will get one in stands crushed (12, two words)

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word for one is placed within the stands
something crushed is mangled out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
an means one

explanation.surface: At these afternoon events, someone gets crushed in the stands.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is French plural, thés dansants, tea dances.
explanation.definitionFit: A thé dansant is an afternoon tea dance, so the plural names afternoon social events.
